extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students and scholars of drama and literary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating poetry and drama (especially tragedy and epic), setting out principles of imitation, plot construction, character, style, and effects such as catharsis. Derived from a theoretical treatise on poetics that defines what makes effective poetic and dramatic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis (imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is an imitation (mimesis) of action, not merely of things, and it imitates by means of rhythm, language, and melody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet imitates universal truths revealed through particular actions; imitation aims to represent life and human action rather than merely copy particular instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; it uses embellished language and incidents arousing pity and fear to achieve catharsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy should present a unified serious action with emotionally powerful incidents and elevated diction; it culminates in purification (catharsis) of audience emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Parts of Tragedy (hierarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy consists of six constituent parts: plot (mythos), character (ethos), thought (dianoia), diction (lexis), melody (melos), and spectacle (opsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is primary (the soul of tragedy), followed by character and thought; diction and melody are means of expression; spectacle is least artistic and relies on stagecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (the arrangement of incidents) is the most important element of tragedy; it determines the whole effect more than character or spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot furnishes the right incidents in the right order to produce the intended emotional effect; characters derive their excellence from their role within the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity/Completeness of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic plot must be complete and whole — it must have a beginning, middle, and end, with incidents so arranged that each follows causally and necessarily from what precedes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid episodic or disjointed sequences; the action should form a single, coherent causal chain so the piece can be grasped as one whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (appropriate length/scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy requires a certain magnitude: the action must be of sufficient size to be complete yet not so long as to lose unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The magnitude should be large enough to permit a full working out of the plot (including reversal/recognition if present) but compact enough to maintain intelligibility and emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness and Elevated Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The action imitated must be serious and important rather than trivial or lowly; the poetic medium should dignify the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy concerns great deeds and calamities affecting persons of high estate or of importance, producing awe and pity in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Necessity (verisimilitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents and speech within the plot must be probable or necessary — they should accord with what is plausible in human affairs and follow by causal necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid improbable contrivances and miracles; recognitions and reversals should arise naturally from the plot's details and causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (tragic error or flaw)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic protagonist typically errs (hamartia) — a mistake or character flaw that brings about his misfortune, rather than pure vice or depravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The error should be natural and intelligible; the hero should not be wholly good or wholly bad, but should evoke both pity and fear through a fall that springs from human frailty or mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal of fortune)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reversal (peripeteia) is a change of the hero's situation from good to bad (or vice versa) that is central to complex plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most artistic reversals are those that arise inevitably from the plot's causal structure rather than by chance; reversal combined with recognition is especially powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition (anagnorisis) is the moment when a character recognizes a previously unknown fact, often linked to peripeteia in complex plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition should be produced by plausible signs or tokens and should deepen the plot logically; it is more artistic when recognition is joined with reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (pity and fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should arouse pity and fear in the audience and effect a catharsis (purging or purification) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The structure and incidents of the drama must be arranged to elicit these emotions appropriately; catharsis is the aesthetic goal and measure of tragic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are complex if they include peripeteia and/or anagnorisis; simple plots lack these and proceed by mere change of fortune without recognition or reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots are generally more artistic because they exhibit the clever interweaving of causation and discovery; simple plots can still be effective if properly unified and probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of Episodes (construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The incidents must be arranged so that the sequence is necessary or probable; the order and connection of episodes is a core part of artistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artful arrangement often involves arranging incidents so that later events follow inevitably from earlier ones, producing emotional and logical satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: Goodness, Consistency, Likeness to Life
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be morally appropriate to the action (neither excessively good nor bad), consistent, and believable as human beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character traits must accord with the parts they play in the plot; inconsistency undermines credibility. Heroes should be superior in some respects but not faultless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (theme, reasoning, and the expression of beliefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought comprises the themes, arguments, and reasoning expressed in speeches — what is said to convey judgments, opinions, or conclusions about action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought should arise naturally from the situation and character and be appropriate to the plot's ethical and intellectual demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Style (language and metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; it includes the choice of words, metaphors, and the use of rhythm and phrasing appropriate to the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style must be clear, elevated, and suitable to the character and situation; metaphor and apt word-choice enhance the poetic effect when they illuminate action or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody / Musical Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (choral song and musical accompaniment) is a structural element that enhances the emotional effect of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music and choral parts should be integrated with the plot and help produce the proper mood; in some genres (e.g., tragedy), melody contributes importantly to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (visual stage effects) as least artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle (opsis) — stagecraft, scenery, and visual display — has great power to affect audiences but is the least artistic element because it depends on external artisanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on spectacle sparingly; the art of tragedy is primarily in plot and character, not in visual effects which are secondary and dependent on production resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the Chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus is not the author of the action but performs a lyric function that complements the plot; it should be integrated but not replace the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chorus provides mood, reflection, and musical interludes; it may comment or amplify but should not carry the main action or resolve key plot problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Miraculous/Contrived Resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots should not be resolved by improbable or miraculous devices (deus ex machina) that break the causal necessity of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolutions should arise from the internal logic of the plot (recognition, reversal, cause), not from arbitrary interventions or unbelievable coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation: Medium, Object, and Manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation differs by medium (verse, prose, spectacle), by object (men in action, character types), and by manner (through narration or enactment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the medium and manner appropriate to the genre: tragedy enacts serious actions (drama), epic narrates over a wider scope with less unity and longer form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences Between Epic and Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and tragedy both imitate but differ in scope, meter, length, and method: epic narrates in verse and can include many episodes, while tragedy enacts a single action with unity and uses dramatic performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epics allow greater breadth and episodic structure; tragedy requires tighter unity and relies on performance, music, and spectacle; poetic diction differs by genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate Use of Recognition Tokens and Probative Details
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions should be produced by plausible tokens, signs, or circumstances that have been laid out in the plot, not by arbitrary revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant evidence early and use it to make recognition credible; this increases the artistic integrity and emotional power of the reversal/recognition.
